edges.relationship: Plutarch’s lives set themselves apart from campaign history, which later critics weigh against Polybius
edges.evidence_note: Plutarch’s opening to Alexander (existing source; opening paragraph read) distinguishes the selected life from a comprehensive campaign history: an ancient statement that campaign history was an established genre from which biography set itself apart. Kromayer (1903, p. 266, read), weighing the sources for Sellasia, prefers Polybius, who had military experience and was near the event, to Plutarch, ‘der … weit- und militärfremde Philosoph von Chäronea’. A comparison of genres; no ancient lineage is claimed for either entry.

edges.relationship: Topographic survey becomes a test of ancient battle narratives (1892–1903)
edges.evidence_note: Grundy’s preface (1901, read): ‘The surveys of Thermopylae, Plataea, and Pylos, I have myself made at different times between 1892 and 1899’; ‘maps without accuracy cannot be used for the historical criticism of highly elaborate narratives’; he signs as ‘University Lecturer in Classical Geography, Oxford’. Kromayer (1903, pp. 1–5, read) finds it surprising that ancient battles were thought manageable without the maps modern war history requires, and takes Moltke’s motto that the locality is ‘das von einer längst vergangenen Begebenheit übriggebliebene Stück Wirklichkeit’; he names Grundy’s surveys as a precedent (p. 3). Polybius had already listed ‘the survey of cities, places, rivers’ as part of history (12.25e). The spatial-history entry dates its own roots to Sauer (1925); this is a comparison of practices, not a claim of influence on that field.

edges.relationship: Liddell Hart attacks documentary and ‘camouflaged’ official military history (1930, 1944)
edges.evidence_note: In-period texts read. The Real War (1930), preface, pp. 9–10 (read in full): ‘a history based solely on formal documents is essentially superficial. Too often, also, it is the unwitting handmaiden of “mythology”.’ Why Don’t We Learn from History? (1944), read in part: ‘Nothing can deceive like a document’ and ‘pure documentary history seems to me akin to mythology’ (pp. 8–9); ‘Many are the gaps to be found in official archives’ (p. 9); ‘History that bears the qualification “official” carries with it a natural reservation; and the additional prefix “military” is apt to imply a double reservation. … This camouflaged history … is the dry rot of armies’ (p. 12). His report of an unnamed German general objecting to the Reichsarchiv history’s frankness (pp. 11–12) is his alone. The target is the official-history practice described in Edmonds’s own preface (1922), not a verdict on any one volume; later studies of the British official history (Green 2003; French 1986) are unread. Distinct from edge_562 (Bassford on Keegan), which joins the same pair.

edges.relationship: Howard judges Liddell Hart’s British Way in Warfare political pamphleteering rather than scholarship (1974)
edges.evidence_note: Mediated: Howard’s 1974 Neale Lecture (The Causes of Wars, p. 172) is unread here and is quoted by Strachan’s 2002 Liddell Hart Centre lecture (read in full), p. 5: ‘A piece of brilliant political pamphleteering, sharply argued, selectively illustrated and [more] concerned to influence British public opinion and government policy than to illuminate the complexities of the past in any serious or scholarly way.’ Strachan adds that ‘The idea of the British way in warfare is not even Liddell Hart’s, it was Julian Corbett’s’ (p. 5), and that the Howard–Paret translation was ‘another breach with Liddell Hart, who had above all been responsible for disseminating that darkness’ about Clausewitz (p. 9). The characterisation of Liddell Hart’s use of history (‘a tool’, p. 2) is Strachan’s. Distinct from edge_561 (Keegan on Clausewitz), which joins the same pair.

edges.relationship: War economy as war history: Hancock’s civil official histories (1941–49)
edges.evidence_note: Mediated, with exact quotation: Morgan-Owen and Finch (2022, pp. 66–67, read) report that W. K. Hancock headed ‘the civil series of the official history of the war’ from 1941, thirty volumes ‘including British War Economy (1949) which he co-authored with Margaret Gowing’, and quote his memoir Country and Calling (1954, pp. 196–97; unread here): ‘the armed forces nowadays were no more than the cutting edge of the nation at war and their history had no higher importance than that of munition making and agriculture, of shipping, land transport, mining and all the other civilian activities.’ A comparison, not a contribution: the economic-history entry does not list Hancock, and British War Economy itself is unread.

verification.note: Read in full for pp. 5–23 for revision 1.142 (evidence-ancient-roots.md §2a), archive.org numbersinhistory00delb. Quoted: ‘We must have historians not only of the Greeks, the Romans, or the Middle Ages, but also specialists for Constitutional History, or Economic History … On this basis, for forty years, I have studied the History of the Art of War’ (pp. 5–6); from the Swiss–Burgundian battles ‘an historian might draw conclusions regarding the course of the battles of Marathon and Plataeae’ (pp. 6–10); Herodotus wrote ‘forty or fifty years after the events’, so that what people tell ‘a generation after will very often be not history, but only legend’ (pp. 8–10); ‘the first point to which in any history of war we have to direct our attention is the number of the warriors’ (p. 11); Thucydides’ figures for Athenian citizen soldiers are ‘subjectively beyond every doubt’, though ‘the interpretation of what the numbers really meant … is not absolutely to be determined’ (pp. 16–17); he questions Caesar’s numbers for the Gauls and Hannibal’s Lacinian inscription reported by Polybius (p. 16); ‘All numbers control each other mutually’, with Moltke’s 1870 deployment as ‘a common standard of measure’ (pp. 17–19); Xerxes’ host (pp. 22–23). verification.note: Read in part for revision 1.142 (evidence-ancient-roots.md §2b), archive.org antikeschlachtfe01krom: Vorwort pp. V–VII; Einleitung pp. 1–7; Mantinea, Beilage I, pp. 90–97 in part; Sellasia, Beilage I, pp. 252–265, and Beilage II, pp. 266–267, in part. Quoted: the book is ‘die Frucht einer Expedition “zur Erforschung antiker Schlachtfelder in Griechenland”’ of spring 1900 with Oberst Janke and ‘Goppel, Hauptmann im Großen Generalstabe’, supported by the Strasbourg faculty, the Berlin Academy and Schlieffen ‘durch Beurlaubung und Ausstattung eines Generalstabsoffiziers’ (Vorwort, signed October 1902); mottoes from Moltke (‘Die Örtlichkeit ist das von einer längst vergangenen Begebenheit übriggebliebene Stück Wirklichkeit’) and Clausewitz; the subject ‘fast allein von Männern genährt …, die von philologisch-historischen Forschungen aus an die Sache herangetreten sind’ (p. 2), with Frederick the Great and Clausewitz quoted for military neglect of antiquity; Grundy’s surveys named as an English precedent (p. 3); the Hellenistic era ‘uns kongenial’ (pp. 5–7, his own presentist framing); Polybius on Ephorus quoted and partly qualified, ‘Polybios’ Urteil setzt bestimmte, aber falsch wiedergegebene Tatsachen in den Berichten des Ephoros voraus’ (pp. 93–96); on Sellasia, Delbrück’s change of view is ‘die Folge meines Vortrages, speziell des Nachweises, daß die Oinusebene weit schmaler ist, als Delbrück, auf ungenaue Reiseberichte gestützt, angenommen hatte’ (p. 252); at stake is ‘die Beurteilung des Polybios und seine Zuverlässigkeit als Kriegschriftsteller und Historiker überhaupt’ (p. 264); Plutarch weighed against Polybius as ‘der … weit- und militärfremde Philosoph von Chäronea’ (p. 266). Delbrück’s side of the dispute (Kriegskunst II and his replies) and Kromayer’s 1900–01 lecture texts are unread; the account of Delbrück’s change of view is Kromayer’s.

verification.note: Read in part for revision 1.142 (evidence-ancient-roots.md §2c) through single-page OCR of a Digital Library of India scan (archive.org 30081001012420): Vorwort pp. V–VI; contents pp. VII–IX; Einleitung pp. 1–3; Kromayer’s ‘Quellen und Literatur’ pp. 14–17. Greek and Roman warfare treated together; Orient, Carthage, Gauls and Germans excluded (‘Wir wollten lieber “multum” als “multa” geben’); strategy and tactics added against ‘der vorwiegend antiquarischen Betrachtungsweise’ (Vorwort). The introduction quotes Veith, who cites Delbrück approvingly on discipline (‘Alle Verschiedenheiten des griechischen und römischen Kriegswesens gehen zurück auf die Verschiedenheit der Disziplin’) and calls the Greek ‘im innersten Wesen unsoldatisch’ (pp. 1–2), national-character generalisations of their time. Arrian ‘sachverständig’, with Ptolemy an equally expert source, and ‘Arrian allein ist militärisch gebildet’ (p. 14); Polybius’ ‘Polemik gegen die Schlachtbeschreibungen älterer Schriftsteller ist jedoch nicht immer gerechtfertigt’ (p. 14); military commentators ‘seit Folard’ projected ‘gewisse militärische Lieblingsideen, Theorien’ onto the ancients (pp. 15–16); ‘Sowohl die historisch-philologische als auch die militärische Fachbildung sind also jede für sich unzureichend’ (p. 16); Hans Droysen (1888–89) on the antiquarian side, Delbrück on ‘der Kunst der Kriegführung’ (p. 17; not Johann Gustav Droysen). Veith’s Roman sections are unread.

edge_039.evidence_note: Clausewitz’s selected text examines judgment and friction; Delbrück’s preface explains mutually checking criticism, and Keegan explicitly uses his work. Mahan and Corbett state maritime purposes. These are named resources, not one uniform origin of military history. Revision 1.142: Delbrück’s London lectures (1913, pp. 5–23, read) make ‘the number of the warriors’ the first point of any history of war and compare numbers across eras; Kromayer (1903, read in part) brings topographic survey to ancient campaigns and disputes Delbrück over Polybius. Strachan (2002 lecture, p. 7, read) calls Delbrück ‘surely the founding father of academic military history’ and says Howard’s War in European History ‘paid obeisance to Delbrück’.

edge_558.evidence_note: Delbrück explicitly credits the 1886 work while correcting estimates. The later teaching umbrella includes this earlier population inquiry; no influence from the 1964 Cambridge Group is backdated. Revision 1.142: Delbrück’s 1913 lectures (pp. 5–23, read) make ‘the number of the warriors’ the first question of military history and weigh Thucydides’ figures for Athenian citizen soldiers as ‘subjectively beyond every doubt’ while their meaning ‘is not absolutely to be determined’ (pp. 16–17); Beloch is not named in the pages read.

edge_853.evidence_note: The atlas’s Military history entry has no Canadian participants. Cook’s account of Stacey and the Army Historical Section (official history as archive-making and narrative) parallels the military entry’s concern with source access and narrative framing. Comparison: the Canadian field is not presented as derived from Howard or Keegan. Revision 1.142 adds an official-history strand to the Military history entry, the international parallel to Cook’s account: Edmonds’s preface (1922, read) describes a Historical Section ‘charged with the sorting and arrangement of the records’ and a history read in proof by officers who took part; Morgan-Owen and Finch (2022, pp. 65–67, read) describe British official commissions during and after the Second World War drawing academic historians to war. Stacey and Duguid stay in the Canadian entry.

edge_064.evidence_note: Strategy and state power create overlapping subjects; no causal direction follows from that overlap. Revision 1.142: Wilkinson’s Oxford inaugural lecture (1909, p. 10, read) holds that ‘in regard to war the architectonic art is policy or politics, not strategy or generalship’.

rationale: The military entry’s dated bar began in 1961 and its only roster rows dated before 1960 were Clausewitz, Nell, Mahan, Delbrück, Corbett, Wedgwood and Roberts; no strand covered official history, campaign and army history from 1898, or the chairs and journals, and no ancient writer appeared anywhere in the graph. The research read the prefaces and front matter of Oman (1898, 1902), Fortescue (1899, 1914), Wilkinson (1909), Edmonds (1922), Liddell Hart (1930, 1944), Fuller (1926), Morison (1947) and Matloff and Snell (1953), and the ancient texts and modern ancient-warfare scholarship (Thucydides, Polybius, Arrian, Vegetius in Latin, Delbrück 1913, Kromayer 1903, Kromayer and Veith 1928, Grundy 1901 and 1911, Parker 1928). Howard’s 1961 lecture is unread and is cited through three readers; Hancock and Maurice are known through Morgan-Owen and Finch (2022), with exact quotations. Ancient writers are precursors of a genre, not a lineage: each ancient claim is recorded where a modern scholar explicitly used or disputed it. Metadata-only and tool-extracted work (Freeman, Falls, Ritter, Ropp, Hintze, Vagts, Tarn, Adcock, Hanson, Lendon, Kaegi 1981, Paret 1991) is deferred, and the thin annales → military edge is not drawn. Wikidata: 18 of 22 new people grounded through the Wikidata MCP; Veith, Parker, Bailey and Cooper are left ungrounded. row.context: Divides systematic history into the study of documents, the survey of places and political experience; holds that no one without experience of war can write well about it; and tests Ephorus’ account of Mantinea against the ground (12.25e–28a). Kromayer (1903, 1928) adopts and qualifies this criticism, and he and Delbrück disputed Polybius’ reliability at Sellasia. Book 12 is fragmentary and polemical.

row.context: Prefers Ptolemy and Aristobulus because they served on Alexander’s campaign, and Ptolemy also because falsehood would have disgraced a king. Kromayer and Veith (1928) call Arrian and Ptolemy expert sources.
row.works: Anabasis of Alexander, preface (Chinnock translation, 1884)

row.context: Joins philology to topographic survey: an expedition to Greek battlefields in spring 1900 with a General Staff officer released by Schlieffen. Defends Polybius against Delbrück at Sellasia (1903), and observes that each era’s military theory shaped its reading of ancient war (1928). His Hellenistic analogies with the modern great state are his own framing.
row.works: Antike Schlachtfelder in Griechenland, vol. I (1903); with Georg Veith, Heerwesen und Kriegführung der Griechen und Römer (1928)

row.context: Co-author of a handbook whose preface treats Greek and Roman warfare together, adds strategy and tactics to the antiquarian study of armies, and excludes the Orient, Carthage, Gauls and Germans. As quoted in its introduction he contrasts Greek and Roman warfare, citing Delbrück on discipline: national-character generalisations of their time. His battlefield volumes are unread.
row.works: With Johannes Kromayer, Heerwesen und Kriegführung der Griechen und Römer (1928)

row.context: Surveyed Thermopylae, Plataea and Pylos himself (1892–99) to test Herodotus and Thucydides, holding that ‘maps without accuracy cannot be used for the historical criticism of highly elaborate narratives’ (1901); his 1911 preface argues that the strategy of the Ten Years’ War is explicable only on economic grounds.
row.works: The Great Persian War (1901), preface; Thucydides and the History of His Age (1911), preface and introduction

row.context: His preface proposes an institutional history of the legions (organisation, recruitment and terms of service), says he has ‘avoided a detailed account of particular campaigns’ and credits Domaszewski and Ritterling; the abbreviation list shows extensive inscription corpora. The body of the book is unread.
row.works: The Roman Legions (1928)

row.context: Compiles earlier authorities (Cato, Celsus, Frontinus, Paternus and imperial constitutions) into what he calls an epitome, and distinguishes such teaching from histories that ‘wrote only the deeds and outcomes of wars’ (the research compiler’s translation of 1.8). Date and published translations not collated.
row.works: Epitoma rei militaris, prologue and 1.8 (Latin text)

row.context: Disputes Delbrück’s criticism of Polybius at Sellasia: textual Sachkritik should not run ahead of topographic survey. He reports that Delbrück changed his view after the plain was shown to be narrower than Delbrück had assumed (1903, Beilage I). Delbrück’s replies are unread.
row.works: Antike Schlachtfelder in Griechenland, vol. I (1903), Beilage I

row.context: Planned a history of the art of war ‘from Greek and Roman times’ (1898), walking battlefields to supplement maps; his Peninsular War (1902) used Record Office papers, including passages omitted from printed dispatches, and treated veterans’ memoirs with ‘very cautious handling’. No influence on or from Delbrück is claimed.
row.works: A History of the Art of War: The Middle Ages (1898), preface; A History of the Peninsular War, vol. I (1902), preface

row.context: A civilian who wrote the army’s history for ‘the political not less than the military aspect’ (1899) and read regimental histories ‘not always with profound respect for their accuracy’. As Trinity College’s first lecturer in military history (1913) he defined it as the strife of communities through ‘organised bands of armed men’, holding that ‘below a certain stage of civilisation, there can be no military history’.
row.works: A History of the British Army, vols. I–II (1899), preface; Military History: Lectures Delivered at Trinity College, Cambridge (1914)

row.context: First Chichele Professor of Military History at Oxford (1909). His inaugural lecture calls military history ‘the effort to understand war’, makes policy, not generalship, ‘the architectonic art’, and holds that ‘as the State is, so will its army be’.
row.works: The University and the Study of War (1909)

row.context: Compiled the British official history of the Western Front in the Committee of Imperial Defence’s Historical Section: ‘based on the British official records’, written partly for ‘students at military schools’, and read in typescript or proof by officers who took part. The preface documents participant review; its effects on the history’s independence are not assessed here. Green (2003) and French (1986) remain unread.
row.works: Military Operations, France and Belgium, 1914, vol. I (1922), preface

row.context: Called history ‘based solely on formal documents’ ‘essentially superficial’ (1930) and official ‘camouflaged history’ ‘the dry rot of armies’ (1944), while placing the war’s decisive history in ‘the cabinets and in the military headquarters’. Strachan (2002) calls him ‘in many ways more a journalist than an academic’, for whom military history was ‘a tool’.
row.works: The Real War, 1914–1918 (1930), preface; Why Don’t We Learn from History? (1944)

row.context: A Harvard historian who proposed a naval history of the war to Roosevelt in 1942 and was given the records he wished to consult; he or his assistants took part in operations. The Navy declared the work ‘in no sense an official history’; Morison held that historians with military experience ‘will always be more tolerant of failure’.
row.works: History of United States Naval Operations in World War II, vol. II, Operations in North African Waters (1947), foreword and introduction

row.context: A former Brooklyn College history instructor who, with Edwin M. Snell, wrote the US Army’s volume on coalition strategic planning; both had served in the war and joined the War Department’s historical project in 1946. row.works: With Edwin M. Snell, Strategic Planning for Coalition Warfare, 1941–1942 (1953)

row.context: Chief Historian of the US Army’s Office of the Chief of Military History, named by Matloff and Snell as ‘the first and most attentive critic’ of their volume. A named editorial role only; his The Historian and the Army (1954) is unread.
row.works: Chief Historian’s review of Matloff and Snell (1953), as acknowledged in their preface

row.context: Headed the civil series of the British official history of the Second World War from 1941; as quoted by Morgan-Owen and Finch, he concluded that the armed forces were ‘no more than the cutting edge of the nation at war’. row.context: Appointed to King’s College London’s new chair of military studies in 1927. row.context: Wanted a ‘science of war’ on which a true history of war would rest (‘We do not want drama; we want truth’) and dismissed Clausewitz’s work as ‘a cloud of flame and smoke’ (1926): history used as a base for theory.
row.works: The Foundations of the Science of War (1926), ch. I §1

row.context: A theorist-historian who used history to argue present policy. strand.title: Official and semi-official history and its critics
strand.focus: General-staff and cabinet historical sections wrote large histories of the world wars from privileged records. Edmonds’s British volumes (from 1922) were ‘based on the British official records’, written partly for ‘students at military schools’ and read in proof by officers who took part. Morison’s naval history was commissioned with full records access yet declared ‘in no sense an official history’ (1947). In the US Army’s series, Matloff and Snell, formerly instructors in history and English respectively and both wartime servicemen, joined the project in 1946; their volume’s foreword, by the Chief of Military History, asked readers to see its controversies as differences ‘among comrades in arms’ (1953), and its preface credits Helen McShane Bailey’s knowledge of the War Department’s records and Evelyn Cooper’s statistics. Liddell Hart attacked documentary and ‘camouflaged’ history (1930, 1944). During and after the Second World War official commissions drew academic historians to war (Hancock and Gowing from 1941, Webster and Frankland from 1950, Howard from 1959), under closure rules and secrecy. Later studies of the genre are unread here, and the German and French official histories are known only from period mentions.

strand.title: Chairs, journals and the soldier-scholar before 1960
strand.focus: In the British institutions examined here, university teaching developed alongside officer education. Oxford made military history a special subject after the South African War, created a lectureship in 1905 and a chair in 1909, whose first holder, Spenser Wilkinson, called military history ‘the effort to understand war’; the chair, vacant from 1939, went to Cyril Falls in 1946 rather than Liddell Hart. Trinity College, Cambridge, appointed Fortescue its first lecturer in military history in 1913. At King’s College London Frederick Maurice held a chair of military studies from 1927; the department closed in 1948. In the United States the American Military History Foundation was incorporated in 1933 after discussions among ‘military and civilian archival personnel’; its journal (1937) became Military Affairs in 1941 and nearly collapsed in 1957. Strachan (2002) calls Liddell Hart and Falls ‘in many ways more a journalist than an academic’ and writes that before Howard’s appointment almost nobody who studied the history of war had not experienced it.
strand.works: Wilkinson, The University and the Study of War (1909); Fortescue, Military History (1914), lecture I; Maurice, ‘On the Uses of the Study of War’ (1927), as quoted by Morgan-Owen and Finch; Society for Military History chronology (1933–69 entries)

strand.title: War, state and society before the ‘new military history’
strand.focus: Wilkinson’s inaugural lecture (1909) held that ‘as the State is, so will its army be’ and that in war ‘the architectonic art is policy or politics, not strategy or generalship’. Maurice (1927, as quoted by Morgan-Owen and Finch) counted statecraft, economics, raw materials, science, industry and civilian morale as of ‘prime importance’ to the study of war. Hancock, editing the civil official histories, treated the armed forces as ‘no more than the cutting edge of the nation at war’ (as quoted by the same authors). Roberts (1955) proposed tactical change with wider institutional effects. Quincy Wright’s foreword (1942) describes a study of war begun at the University of Chicago in 1926 that involved ‘over fifty studies by research assistants and members of the faculty’; only the foreword is read. Karsten (1984) calls such questions the ‘new’ military history while conceding that ‘some scholars explored such questions in the past’. Hintze, Vagts, Ritter and Ropp are not yet read for this entry.
strand.works: Wilkinson (1909); Maurice, inaugural lecture (1927); Wright, A Study of War (1942), foreword; Hancock and Gowing, British War Economy (1949); Roberts, ‘The Military Revolution, 1560–1660’ (1955 lecture); Karsten (1984), opening

strand.title: Ancient historians on testimony, terrain and experience
strand.focus: Thucydides tests eyewitness accounts against one another and says Spartan secrecy and bragging prevent accurate numbers at Mantinea. Polybius requires the study of documents, the survey of places and political experience, holds that no one without experience of war can write well about it, and judges Ephorus’ land battles by the ground; his polemic is also self-promotion. Arrian prefers Ptolemy and Aristobulus because they served on the campaign. Grundy (1911) calls Thucydides’ narrative ‘in the main a military history’ subordinated to political teaching, and Kromayer (1903) adopts and qualifies Polybius’ criticism of Ephorus. Delbrück (1913, p. 16) asks: ‘Ought we to believe what Caesar informs us of concerning the gigantic armies of the Gauls, whose conquest is his glory, since we have now seen that neither Napoleon nor Frederick in this respect is to be trusted?’; Caesar’s text itself was not read. Herodotus and Xenophon appear only through modern critics: Delbrück (1913) notes that Herodotus wrote ‘forty or fifty years after the events’, Grundy (1901) that in military matters he ‘seems to have possessed little, if any, special knowledge’, and Kromayer (1903, p. 93) finds Xenophon’s account of Mantinea one-sided. These writers are precursors of a genre, not a single origin of the field.
strand.works: Thucydides, History 1.22, 5.68; Polybius, Histories 12.25e–28a, 3.33, 3.48; Arrian, Anabasis, preface; Grundy (1901), preface, and (1911), pp. 7–9; Kromayer (1903), pp. 93–96; Delbrück, Numbers in History (1913), pp. 8–10, 16

strand.title: Battlefield survey, numbers and the Delbrück–Kromayer dispute
strand.focus: Grundy’s surveys of Thermopylae, Plataea and Pylos (1892–99) and Kromayer’s expedition to Greek battlefields with General Staff officers (1900) test ancient narratives against terrain; Delbrück’s London lectures (1913) test numbers by comparison across eras, with Moltke’s 1870 deployment as a measure. At Sellasia Delbrück and Kromayer disagreed over Polybius’ reliability and over whether criticism may run ahead of survey; the claim that Delbrück changed his view after Kromayer’s survey is Kromayer’s (1903), and Delbrück’s replies are unread. Kromayer framed the work against Clausewitz’s judgment that ancient military history was the least useful.
strand.works: Grundy, The Great Persian War (1901), preface; Kromayer, Antike Schlachtfelder in Griechenland I (1903), Einleitung and Beilage I; Delbrück, Numbers in History (1913); Clausewitz, On War, II.6

strand.title: Interwar theorist-historians and the uses of history
strand.focus: Fuller wanted a ‘science of war’, called the history of war ‘a great romance’ without one, and dismissed Clausewitz’s work as ‘a cloud of flame and smoke’ (1926). Liddell Hart used history to argue present policy and attacked official history (1930, 1944); Strachan (2002) writes that for him military history was ‘a tool, a tool to communicate ideas about war that had present application’. Howard (1974, as quoted by Strachan) judged The British Way in Warfare ‘brilliant political pamphleteering’, and Strachan credits the idea to Corbett.
strand.works: Fuller, The Foundations of the Science of War (1926), ch. I; Liddell Hart, The Real War (1930) and Why Don’t We Learn from History? (1944); Howard, 1974 Neale Lecture, as quoted by Strachan (2002)
